quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Stranded Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: In 'The receptionist I spoke to was really helpful,' what has happened to the relative clause?
quests.targetClause: The preposition 'to' has stayed at the end of the clause, and the relative pronoun has been omitted.
quests.completedSentence: In 'The receptionist I spoke to was really helpful,' what has happened to the relative clause?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'To' goes with the verb 'spoke' (spoke to someone). It has stayed at the end of the clause - a natural pattern in everyday English - and the object relative pronoun ('who,' 'whom,' or 'that') has simply been dropped, as it can be in defining clauses.
quests.nativeTip: Ask which verb 'to' belongs with, and what could be inserted after 'receptionist' without changing the meaning.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The preposition 'to' has stayed at the end of the clause, and the relative pronoun has been omitted."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Stranded Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: The clinic ___ my mother works at closes at six.
quests.targetClause: that
quests.completedSentence: The clinic that my mother works at closes at six.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'At' has stayed at the end of the clause, so the relative word only has to stand for 'the clinic' as the object of that preposition: 'that' does this. 'Where' and 'in which' would repeat the idea of location, and 'whom' is for people.
quests.nativeTip: The preposition 'at' is already sitting at the end of the clause. Which option can work alongside it without repeating the idea of place?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "that"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Stranded Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which one of these sentences is grammatically correct?
quests.targetClause: The topic we talked about was fascinating.
quests.completedSentence: Which one of these sentences is grammatically correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Talk about' needs its preposition, which stays at the end when the pronoun is dropped. Leaving it out is an error, adding 'it' repeats the topic, and placing 'about' in front of 'we' without 'which' leaves the clause incomplete.
quests.nativeTip: The verb 'talked' needs its preposition, and 'the topic' is already represented by the relative clause - it should not be repeated.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The topic we talked about was fascinating."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: Compare: A) 'The receptionist I spoke to was very helpful.' B) 'The receptionist to whom I spoke was very helpful.' What is the main difference?
quests.targetClause: In B the preposition has moved in front of 'whom,' which gives a more formal tone.
quests.completedSentence: Compare: A) 'The receptionist I spoke to was very helpful.' B) 'The receptionist to whom I spoke was very helpful.' What is the main difference?
quests.ruleExplanation: Both sentences are grammatical and mean the same thing. In B the preposition has moved in front of 'whom,' which gives a more formal, written tone; A keeps the preposition at the end, which is natural in speech.
quests.nativeTip: Compare where 'to' sits in each sentence, and think about which version you would hear in a casual conversation.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "In B the preposition has moved in front of 'whom,' which gives a more formal tone."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: The company ___ I work has offices in three countries.
quests.targetClause: for which
quests.completedSentence: The company for which I work has offices in three countries.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For which' is correct: the preposition of 'work for' moves in front of 'which' because a company is a thing. 'For that' and 'for who' are never possible, and 'which for' puts the preposition in the wrong place.
quests.nativeTip: A preposition placed before the relative pronoun can only be followed by one of two pronouns - pick the one that suits a company.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "for which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: The colleague ___ I sent the report has not replied yet.
quests.targetClause: to whom
quests.completedSentence: The colleague to whom I sent the report has not replied yet.
quests.ruleExplanation: A fronted preposition takes 'whom' (never 'who') for a person: 'to whom I sent the report.' 'To who' is a frequent error, 'to that' is never allowed, and 'whom to' reverses the order.
quests.nativeTip: A person as the antecedent plus a fronted preposition calls for the object form of 'who.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "to whom"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: Which of these relative pronouns can never come directly after a preposition such as 'to' or 'with'?
quests.targetClause: that
quests.completedSentence: Which of these relative pronouns can never come directly after a preposition such as 'to' or 'with'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' cannot follow a preposition: we say 'the pen with which she wrote,' never 'the pen with that she wrote.' 'Whom,' 'which,' and 'whose' can all follow a preposition.
quests.nativeTip: Think of phrases like 'to whom,' 'in which,' and 'with whose help.' One common relative pronoun never appears in that position.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "that"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: The tool with ___ she repaired the engine was designed in Japan.
quests.targetClause: which
quests.completedSentence: The tool with which she repaired the engine was designed in Japan.
quests.ruleExplanation: After a preposition, the relative pronoun must be 'whom' for people or 'which' for things. A tool is a thing, so 'with which' is correct; 'with that' and 'with who' are never possible.
quests.nativeTip: A preposition sits right before the gap, and the antecedent is a tool. Which pronoun is allowed here?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: The doctor with ___ my sister trained is now head of surgery.
quests.targetClause: whom
quests.completedSentence: The doctor with whom my sister trained is now head of surgery.
quests.ruleExplanation: After a preposition, a person takes 'whom': 'with whom my sister trained.' 'Who' and 'that' cannot follow a preposition, and 'which' is reserved for things.
quests.nativeTip: The antecedent is a person, and a preposition sits right before the gap.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "whom"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Choosing the Correct Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Choosing the Correct Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: The club ___ which he belongs meets on Fridays.
quests.targetClause: to
quests.completedSentence: The club to which he belongs meets on Fridays.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Belong' takes 'to' (belong to a club), and that preposition moves in front of 'which' in the formal pattern: 'to which he belongs.'
quests.nativeTip: Ask which preposition the verb 'belong' normally takes - the preposition is chosen by the verb, not by the relative pronoun.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "to"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Choosing the Correct Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Choosing the Correct Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: The friend I can always rely ___ lives abroad.
quests.targetClause: on
quests.completedSentence: The friend I can always rely on lives abroad.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Rely' takes 'on.' Because the relative pronoun has been dropped, the preposition stays at the end of the clause: 'the friend I can always rely on.'
quests.nativeTip: Complete the phrase inside the clause as if the friend were the object: 'I can rely ___ my friend.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "on"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Choosing the Correct Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Choosing the Correct Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: The mistake she is responsible ___ cost the firm thousands of dollars.
quests.targetClause: for
quests.completedSentence: The mistake she is responsible for cost the firm thousands of dollars.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Responsible' takes 'for.' Adjective-plus-preposition pairs work like verb-plus-preposition pairs inside a relative clause: the preposition stays with its word even when the noun is moved to the front.
quests.nativeTip: Prepositions also attach to adjectives. What follows 'responsible' in 'she is responsible ___ the mistake'?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "for"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: Which of these sentences is correctly formed?
quests.targetClause: The person to whom I spoke was helpful.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these sentences is correctly formed?
quests.ruleExplanation: With the preposition in front, the pronoun must stay and must be 'whom' for a person. Dropping it, reversing the order, or using 'which' for a person all break the pattern.
quests.nativeTip: When the preposition comes first, the relative pronoun cannot be dropped - and it must suit the antecedent.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The person to whom I spoke was helpful."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is NOT acceptable in standard English?
quests.targetClause: The book for I was looking is out of stock.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is NOT acceptable in standard English?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For I was looking' puts the preposition in front with no relative pronoun after it, which is never possible. The other three are all acceptable: pronoun dropped, 'that' kept, or 'for which' fronted.
quests.nativeTip: Three of these are the same idea in different registers. One breaks a rule about fronted prepositions.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The book for I was looking is out of stock."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission with Stranded Prepositions
quests.questionSentence: If you delete the relative pronoun, which sentence stays grammatical?
quests.targetClause: The colleague whom I share an office with is retiring.
quests.completedSentence: If you delete the relative pronoun, which sentence stays grammatical?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The colleague I share an office with' is fine: 'whom' is an object pronoun in a defining clause with a stranded preposition. Deleting 'whom' after a fronted preposition breaks the sentence, a subject pronoun cannot be dropped, and a non-defining clause must keep its pronoun.
quests.nativeTip: Delete the pronoun in each sentence and read what is left. Watch for fronted prepositions, subject clauses, and commas.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The colleague whom I share an office with is retiring."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Spoken vs Formal Preposition Placement
quests.questionSentence: You are chatting with a friend about a restaurant. Which sentence sounds most natural?
quests.targetClause: That's the place I was telling you about.
quests.completedSentence: You are chatting with a friend about a restaurant. Which sentence sounds most natural?
quests.ruleExplanation: In casual conversation, people leave the preposition at the end and drop the relative pronoun: 'the place I was telling you about.' The fronted version sounds like a written text, 'about that' is ungrammatical, and 'whom' cannot refer to a place.
quests.nativeTip: Everyday speech keeps the preposition at the end and tends to drop the pronoun.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "That's the place I was telling you about."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Spoken vs Formal Preposition Placement
quests.questionSentence: In a formal legal letter, which phrasing is most appropriate?
quests.targetClause: The tenant to whom the notice was addressed has not responded.
quests.completedSentence: In a formal legal letter, which phrasing is most appropriate?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'To whom' is the most formal way to express this relationship. The other versions are grammatical but conversational, and one of them uses a contraction, which a legal letter would avoid.
quests.nativeTip: Formal writing tends to move the preposition to the front and use 'whom' or 'which.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The tenant to whom the notice was addressed has not responded."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Spoken vs Formal Preposition Placement
quests.questionSentence: Which line would sound out of place in a casual voicemail message?
quests.targetClause: The guy to whom I spoke this morning said he'd call you back.
quests.completedSentence: Which line would sound out of place in a casual voicemail message?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'To whom I spoke' is a formal, written pattern and would sound stiff in a voicemail. The other lines keep the preposition at the end, which is how people naturally speak.
quests.nativeTip: Think about which version sounds like a letter rather than a phone message.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The guy to whom I spoke this morning said he'd call you back."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Stranded Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The company I work is based in Leeds.'
quests.targetClause: The preposition 'for' has been left out of the relative clause.
quests.completedSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The company I work is based in Leeds.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Work for' needs its preposition. When the relative pronoun is dropped, the preposition still has to stay in the clause: 'The company I work for is based in Leeds.'
quests.nativeTip: Complete the clause as if it were a normal sentence: 'I work ___ the company.' What is missing?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The preposition 'for' has been left out of the relative clause."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The manager to whom I reported to resigned.'
quests.targetClause: The preposition 'to' appears twice - before 'whom' and again at the end.
quests.completedSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The manager to whom I reported to resigned.'
quests.ruleExplanation: The preposition 'to' has been used twice: once before 'whom' and again at the end of the clause. It should appear only once - 'to whom I reported' or 'whom I reported to.'
quests.nativeTip: Count how many times the preposition appears. A preposition belongs in only one place.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The preposition 'to' appears twice - before 'whom' and again at the end."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Choosing the Correct Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Choosing the Correct Preposition in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence contains a wrong preposition?
quests.targetClause: The friend I depend to lives nearby.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence contains a wrong preposition?
quests.ruleExplanation: We say 'depend on,' not 'depend to.' The other sentences use the correct prepositions: stay at a hotel, rely on a tool, dance to a song.
quests.nativeTip: Say each verb phrase on its own - depend ___, rely ___, stay ___, dance ___ - and see which pairing does not exist.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The friend I depend to lives nearby."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses with Prepositions
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is correct, given that I have only one manager?
quests.targetClause: My manager, to whom I report weekly, is on leave.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is correct, given that I have only one manager?
quests.ruleExplanation: With only one manager, the clause is non-defining and needs commas on both sides. After the preposition, only 'whom' (or 'which' for things) is possible - not 'who' or 'that.' Removing the commas would suggest several managers.
quests.nativeTip: One manager means the clause is extra information - check the commas, and remember which pronouns may follow a preposition.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "My manager, to whom I report weekly, is on leave."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses with Prepositions
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is correct, given that the company has only one founder?
quests.targetClause: Our founder, whom everyone looks up to, is retiring.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is correct, given that the company has only one founder?
quests.ruleExplanation: The single founder makes the clause non-defining: it needs both commas and a visible pronoun, and 'that' cannot follow a comma. 'Whom everyone looks up to' keeps the preposition at the end, which is natural.
quests.nativeTip: A non-defining clause needs commas on both sides, and its pronoun cannot be dropped even when the preposition stays at the end.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Our founder, whom everyone looks up to, is retiring."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses with Prepositions
quests.questionSentence: Which of these versions of the sentence is ungrammatical?
quests.targetClause: The conference, at that the CEO announced the merger, was held in Lisbon.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these versions of the sentence is ungrammatical?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'At that' is impossible: a pronoun following a preposition must be 'whom' or 'which.' 'At which,' 'which ... at,' and 'where' are all acceptable ways to say the same thing.
quests.nativeTip: Three versions express the same idea in different ways. Look for the one that puts a forbidden pronoun after the preposition.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The conference, at that the CEO announced the merger, was held in Lisbon."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + which as Formal Alternative to where
quests.grammarRule: Preposition + which as Formal Alternative to where
quests.questionSentence: Which phrase can replace 'where' in 'The house where I grew up was demolished' without changing the meaning?
quests.targetClause: in which
quests.completedSentence: Which phrase can replace 'where' in 'The house where I grew up was demolished' without changing the meaning?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Where' is shorthand for 'in which' - the preposition and the pronoun together. 'Which in' reverses the order, and 'in that' is not possible after a preposition.
quests.nativeTip: Think about what 'where' stands for: a place plus the preposition that goes with it.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "in which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + which as Formal Alternative to when
quests.grammarRule: Preposition + which as Formal Alternative to when
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is correct?
quests.targetClause: The day on which we met was a Tuesday.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'On which' is the formal equivalent of 'when' for a day. 'On that' and 'on who' are impossible after a preposition, and adding 'it' after 'on' repeats the noun.
quests.nativeTip: This is the time version of the same pattern: a preposition followed by 'which.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The day on which we met was a Tuesday."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + which as Formal Alternative to where
quests.grammarRule: Preposition + which as Formal Alternative to where
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is incorrect?
quests.targetClause: The city in which she was born in is small.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is incorrect?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'In which she was born in' repeats the preposition. The other versions use it once: fronted ('in which'), stranded ('she was born in'), or replaced by 'where.'
quests.nativeTip: Three sentences say the same thing in different ways. Check whether any of them uses the preposition twice.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The city in which she was born in is small."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: In a formal complaint letter, the writer says: 'The manager ___ I submitted my complaint never replied.'
quests.targetClause: to whom
quests.completedSentence: In a formal complaint letter, the writer says: 'The manager to whom I submitted my complaint never replied.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'To whom' is correct: the complaint was submitted to the manager, the preposition moves to the front, and a person after a preposition takes 'whom.' 'To which' is for things, and 'to who' is never used.
quests.nativeTip: A fronted preposition, a person as the antecedent, and a formal setting all point to the same choice.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "to whom"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence has something wrong with it?
quests.targetClause: The person with who I was talking seemed nervous.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence has something wrong with it?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'With who' is incorrect: a pronoun following a preposition must be 'whom.' The other sentences are fine - dropped pronoun, fronted 'with whom,' and stranded 'whom ... to.'
quests.nativeTip: Three sentences are just different registers of one idea. Check which pronoun follows the preposition in the odd one out.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The person with who I was talking seemed nervous."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + whom/which (Fronted Preposition)
quests.questionSentence: Which statement about prepositions in relative clauses is FALSE?
quests.targetClause: When the preposition comes before the relative pronoun, the pronoun can be dropped.
quests.completedSentence: Which statement about prepositions in relative clauses is FALSE?
quests.ruleExplanation: When the preposition comes before the pronoun, the pronoun can never be dropped. The other three statements are true: stranded prepositions are natural in everyday English, fronted ones require 'whom' or 'which,' and non-defining clauses always keep their pronoun.
quests.nativeTip: Test each statement against what you know about fronted prepositions, stranded prepositions, and omission.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "When the preposition comes before the relative pronoun, the pronoun can be dropped."
